text: Scene 2 - Visit to Lord Fermor
speaker: C5

text: At half-past twelve next day Lord Henry Wotton strolled from Curzon Street over to the Albany to call on his uncle, Lord Fermor,
speaker: Lord Henery

text: a genial if somewhat ill mannered old man
speaker: C5

text: whom the outside world called selfish because it derived no particular benefit from him, but who was considered generous by Society as he fed the people who amused him.
speaker: C6

text: He had two large town houses but preferred to live in chambers as it was less trouble and he took most of his meals at his club.
speaker: C4

text: He was a hero to his valet, who bullied him, and a terror to most of his relations, whom he bullied in turn.
speaker: C8

text: Only England could have produced him, and he always said that the country was going to the dogs.
speaker: C5

text: His principles were out of date, but there was a good deal to be said for his prejudices.
speaker: C6

text: When Lord Henry entered the room,
speaker: Lord Henery

text: He found his uncle sitting in a rough shooting-coat, smoking a cheroot and grumbling over The Times.
speaker: Lord F

text: Well, Harry, what brings you out so early? I thought you dandies never got up till two, and were not visible till five.
speaker: Lord F

text: Pure family affection, I assure you, Uncle George. I want to get something out of you.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Money, I suppose, Well, sit down and tell me all about it.
speaker: Lord F

text: I don't want money Uncle. It’s only people who pay their bills who want that. I want information: not useful information, of course; useless information.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Well, I can tell you anything that is in an English Blue Book, Harry, although those fellows nowadays write a lot of nonsense.
speaker: Lord F

text: Mr. Dorian Gray does not belong to Blue Books, Uncle George.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Mr. Dorian Gray? Who is he?
speaker: Lord F

text: He is the late Lord Kelso's grandson. I want you to tell me all about his mother.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Kelso’s grandson! Yes I knew his mother - Margaret Devereux. She made all the men frantic by running away with a penniless young fellow - a mere nobody, sir, a subaltern in a foot regiment, or something of that kind. The poor chap was killed in a duel at Spa a few months after the marriage. They said Kelso got some rascally adventurer, to insult his son-in-law in public… paid him, sir, to do it, paid him! The fellow spitted his man as if he had been a pigeon. The thing was hushed up, but, egad, Kelso ate his chop alone at the club for some time afterwards. He brought his daughter back with him, I was told, and she never spoke to him again. She died within a year. So she left a son, did she? What sort of boy is he? If he is like his mother, he must be a good-looking chap.
speaker: Lord F

text: He is very good-looking.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: I hope he will fall into proper hands. He should have a pot of money waiting for him if Kelso did the right thing by him. His mother had money, too. All the Selby property came to her.
speaker: Lord F

text: His mother was very beautiful?
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Margaret Devereux was one of the loveliest creatures I ever saw, Harry.
speaker: Lord F

text: Thank you Uncle George. I always like to know everything about my new friends, and nothing about my old ones. Now I must say good-bye or I shall be late for lunch.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Where are you lunching, Harry?
speaker: Lord F

text: At Aunt Agatha's. I have asked myself and Mr. Gray. He is her latest protege.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Humph! tell your Aunt Agatha, Harry, not to bother me any more with her charity appeals. I am sick of them. Why, the good woman thinks that I have nothing to do but to write cheques for her silly fads.
speaker: Lord F

text: All right, Uncle George, I'll tell her, but it won't have any effect. Philanthropic people lose all sense of humanity. It is their distinguishing characteristic.
speaker: Lord Henery
